title: Ascension Day

segments.voice: Yesterday, Rogation days: walking the edges and asking for the harvest. Your line was beating the bounds.

A small group of friends stands on a hill outside Jerusalem, heads tipped back, staring at an empty sky. A moment ago Jesus was talking with them. Then he was lifted up, and a cloud took him out of their sight. It's the stance of someone left on a platform after the train has gone. Then two men in white are beside them, and in the King James Bible they ask a fair question: "Ye men of Galilee, why stand ye gazing up into heaven?" Acts sets this after forty days of Jesus appearing to his friends. Today, Ascension Day.

Acts says the risen Jesus was "seen of them forty days, and speaking of the things pertaining to the kingdom of God." That's where the feast's timing comes from. Then the hill: "while they beheld, he was taken up; and a cloud received him out of their sight." In the Bible a cloud can be more than weather. It's how God's presence shows up and hides at once, over the mountain, over the tent in the desert. So the cloud isn't saying he got lost in the sky. Christians say he went into God's presence, and the old creeds say it too: he ascended into heaven, and sits at the right hand of the Father. Churches understand that differently, some picturing an upward journey, some hearing "up" as the only word we have for going into God. Either way, in the texts it isn't a goodbye. Luke ends his Gospel: "they worshipped him, and returned to Jerusalem with great joy." Not grief. Joy. Set that beside Matthew, who doesn't tell the Ascension at all and ends with a promise: "lo, I am with you alway, even unto the end of the world." Some Christians put it this way: at the Ascension, Jesus stops being in one place so he can be with his friends everywhere. Then the angels' question does its work. Stop staring up. Go back to the city. There's a wait coming, and then a job. Look up, then get on with it.

Go to a window or step outside if you can, look up at whatever's there, sky, ceiling, clouds, and let your shoulders drop. If you pray, hold Matthew's line in the quiet, lo, I am with you alway; if you don't, notice the size of the sky over your small day. Then bring your eyes down to the next ordinary thing in front of you.
Ascension Day. Forty days after Easter, the feast of Jesus taken up into God's presence, and the promise that he stays with his friends.
Your line: he is with you always. They went back to the city with joy, not grief. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Churches that keep Ascension Day mark it forty days after Easter with a service reading the end of Luke and the start of Acts; some move the celebration to the following Sunday.
